column2: Therefore, because of that curse, whenever dharma perishes he is born again and again here among men for the welfare of all worlds.
Having spoken thus to Vishnu, he himself took up her head, brought it back, joined it to the body, and said:

You who were truly slain by Vishnu, I now restore to life, if the whole of dharma has been practised by me or is known by me.
brahmandpuran:110:146	By that truth, live — if I speak the truth. By his utterance of truth the goddess was then brought back to life.
Sprinkling her with cool water, he said, "Live!" Then, as all beings saw her rise as though from sleep,
voices of unseen beings resounded in all directions, crying "Well done, well done!" Seeing the goddess thus revived by Bhrigu,
it seemed a marvel to all beings who watched. Then, seeing his wife revived by the unperturbed Bhrigu,
Indra found no peace for fear of Kavya. Lying awake, Indra, chastiser of Paka, spoke to his own daughter Jayanti,
the wise one addressing his maiden: "This Kavya is performing terrible austerities to deprive me of my Indra-hood.
By him I have been greatly troubled, my daughter, though my mind is firm. Go, O auspicious one, and attend on him with services that relieve his fatigue,
tirelessly, with every attention pleasing to his mind." The goddess Jayanti, daughter of Indra, of virtuous conduct,
assuming a lovely form, went to him who was keeping that hard vow, and did for Kavya just as her father had told her.
Sweet of speech, she praised him with pleasing words, and served him at the proper times by gently massaging his limbs;
attending on him agreeably, she stayed for many years. When the terrible thousand-year vow of drinking smoke was complete,
Shiva, pleased, offered Kavya a boon: "This vow has been completed by you alone and by no one else.
Therefore by austerity, intellect, learning, strength and splendour you will surpass all the gods.
Whatever Veda is mine, O joy of Bhrigu's line, with its limbs and secrets, and the Upanishads of sacrifice —
all of it will be revealed to you, but it must not be told to anyone. Thereby you will become the best of the twice-born, surpassing all."
Having given this boon to the Bhargava, Bhava further granted him lordship over creatures, lordship over wealth and invulnerability.
Obtaining these boons, Kavya's hair stood on end with joy, and out of that joy a divine hymn to the great Lord sprang forth from him.
Then, standing aslant, he praised the blue-red god thus: Salutation to the dark-throated one, the first of the gods, the radiant one,
to the one who licks and is to be licked, to the Year, O lord of the world, to the one with matted hair and hair standing up, giver of boons to the tawny-eyed one,
to the one well praised, the holy ford, the god of gods, the swift one, the turbaned one, the fair-faced one, the thousand-eyed, the bountiful,
to Rudra whose seed is wealth, to Austerity, to the one clad in rags, to the one without possessions, with loose hair, to the commander of armies, to the red one,
to the seer, the elder of kings, the one who plays with Takshaka, the mountain-dweller with the sun for an eye, the ascetic, the drinker of ghee,
to the well-rounded, the fair-handed, the bowman, the Bhargava, the thousand-armed, the one with a thousand pure eyes,
the thousand-bellied, the thousand-footed, the thousand-headed, the many-formed creator,
to Bhava, the universal form, the white one, the Person, the bearer of the quiver, the armoured, the subtle, the destroyer,
to the copper-coloured, the terrible, the fierce, the auspicious, to Mahadeva, to Sharva, to the auspicious one of universal form,
to the golden, the most excellent, the rain, the middle one, the abode, the tawny, the reddish-brown and the ruddy one,
to the bearer of Pinaka, the archer, the variegated, the red one, the one of the drum, the one-footed, the worthy, the Intellect, the hunter of the deer, Sharva, the pillar, the fearsome,
to the many-formed, the fierce, the three-eyed, the Lord, the tawny one, the sole hero, Death, the three-eyed Tryambaka,
to the lord of the dwelling, the bow Pinaka, Shankara and Shiva, the forest-dweller, the householder, the ascetic, the celibate student,
to Sankhya and to Yoga, the meditator, the initiated, the hidden, Sharva, the one to be worshipped with austerity, the all-pervading,
to the awakened, the pure, the liberated, the absolute, the bank, the one who is aware, the foremost knower of Brahman, the great sage,
the four-footed, the pure for sacrifice, the armoured, the swift, the one with a crest, the skull-bearer, the staff-bearer, the all-wise,
the incomprehensible, the blazing, the sun, the wise, the cruel, the deformed, the loathsome and the auspicious,
the pure, the garment, the one born at once (Sadyojata), Death, the eater of flesh, Sharva, the cloud and the lightning,
to Daksha and to the last-born, the lord of the worlds, the one free from sickness, the fuel, the golden, the one-eyed,
to the best, to Vamadeva and Ishana, the wise, the great Kalpa, the blazing, the weeping one and the laughing one,
the firm-bowed, the armoured, the chariot-rider, the protector, the lord of the Bhrigus, Shukra, the dweller in caves, the wise,
the unfailing, the tranquil, ever dear to brahmins — sky-clad, clad in hide, destroyer of Bhaga, salutation to you!
Salutation to the lord of creatures, the lord of beings, the source of Rig, Yajus and Saman, to Svaha and to Svadha,
to the supreme Vashat call, to you whose self is the mantra, salutation. To the creator, the sustainer, the maker, the remover and the destroyer,
lord of past, future and present, to you whose self is action, salutation. To the Vasus, the Sadhyas, the Rudras, the Adityas and the Ashvins,
to the Vishvedevas and the Maruts, to you whose self is the gods, salutation. To the knower of the rites of Agni and Soma, the victim, the mantra and the herb,
to the sacrificial fee and the concluding bath, to you whose self is the sacrifice, salutation. To austerity and truth, renunciation and tranquillity,
to non-violence and non-greed, the well-dressed and the sleepless, arisen from all beings, to you whose self is yoga, salutation.
To the earth, the atmosphere, the Mahar and heavenly worlds, the Jana, Tapas and Satya worlds, to you whose self is the worlds, salutation.
To the unmanifest, the Mahat, the elements and the senses, the subtle elements and the great, to you whose self is the principles, salutation.
To the eternal, the markless, the subtle and the other, the pure and all-pervading, to you whose self is eternal, salutation.
Salutation to you in the three worlds ending with Svar, beginning with Bhuvar, and in the four beginning with Mahar and ending with Satya, salutation to you.
Whatever I have spoken wrongly in this hymn of names, O Lord, forgive it all, O friend of brahmins, since I am your devotee.
His aim accomplished, the joyful one resumed his own form; knowing the Asuras to be ruined, he vanished, his purpose achieved.
When he had vanished, the Danavas were bewildered and said to one another, "Alas, shame! We have been deceived through affection.
We were made to turn from dharma by the Creator, and burned by trickery in our own affairs through illusion."
Then the Asuras, terrified of the gods, hurried away, and with Prahlada at their head again followed Kavya.
Reaching Kavya, they stood before him with downcast faces. Seeing them come back, Kavya spoke to his disciples:
I advised you in time, yet you did not heed me; through that arrogance you have met with defeat.
Prahlada then said to him, "Give up your wounded pride, O Bhargava, toward your own disciples who worship you and are especially devoted.
While you were away we were deluded by the preceptor of the gods. Seeing this with your far-reaching vision, you ought to protect us, your devotees.
If you do not show us grace, O joy of Bhrigu's line, then, rejected by you, we shall enter Rasatala today."
Suta said: Understanding the truth of the matter, Kavya, conciliated thus, out of his great compassion set aside his anger.
He said: "Do not fear, and do not go to Rasatala. This outcome was inevitable; it befell you even while I was watching.
It cannot be made otherwise, for destiny is stronger. The consciousness that you have lost you shall surely regain.
'The time of turning has come,' Brahma declared. By my grace you enjoyed the mighty three worlds
for ten full ages, standing on the heads of the gods; Brahma declared that your rule would last just that long.
In the Savarni age the kingdom shall again be yours; your grandson Bali shall once more be lord of the worlds.
Thus the time for your grandson was declared by Brahma himself. So even when the worlds were taken from him, he felt no grief.
Because his actions were not bound by desires, the pleased Unborn One granted that in the Savarni interval
the kingdom of the gods would be Bali's — so the Lord told me. Therefore he remains unseen by beings, awaiting his time.
The pleased Self-born also granted you immortality; so do not be anxious or suddenly troubled about the turn of events.
I cannot move ahead of this for your sake; I am forbidden by Brahma, who knows the future, O lord.
These two disciples of mine, equal to Brihaspati, will sustain all of you in your conflict with the gods."
Suta said: Thus addressed by Kavya of unwearied deeds, the Daityas led by Prahlada went off with those two.
The Daityas and Danavas, hearing of that inevitable outcome, eagerly proclaimed the victory Kavya had foretold.
Armoured and armed, they all challenged the gods. Seeing the Asuras present for battle,
the gods, clad in armour, fought them. The war of gods and Asuras went on for a hundred years; the Asuras defeated the gods, and the defeated gods took counsel.
The gods said: We have been defeated by the Asuras through the power of Shanda and Amarka. So, with a sacrifice in view, let us do what is to our own benefit.
We shall invite them to the sacrifice and then defeat the Asuras. Then the gods invited both Shanda and Amarka.
Calling the two brahmins to the sacrifice, they said, "Abandon the Asuras.
We will offer you a cup of Soma once we have conquered the Danavas." So Shanda and Amarka then abandoned the Asuras for the gods.
Then the gods won victory and the Danavas suffered defeat; having defeated the Asuras, the gods drew near Shanda and Amarka.
Overcome by Kavya's curse and left without support, the Asuras, harassed by the gods, entered Rasatala.
Thus the Danavas were made powerless by Indra. From that time, through the curse caused by Bhrigu,
the Lord Vishnu is born again and again whenever sacrifice declines, to establish dharma and destroy adharma.
The Asuras who did not abide by Prahlada's command — the Lord Brahma declared that all of them could be slain by men.
Therefore Narayana was born of Dharma in the Chakshusha interval; and Vainya (Prithu) established sacrifice in the Vaivasvata interval.
At the manifestation of Vainya, Brahma himself was the priest. In the fourth age, when the gods were in distress,
he was born within the ocean to slay Hiranyakashipu. The second was Narasimha, fierce, with Suta as priest.
To the lord of the Daityas who was performing a sacrifice, the joy of Aditi's family, having become a brahmin at an auspicious time, spoke to Bali, son of Virochana:
You are king of the three worlds; everything rests in you. O king, you ought to give me three strides, said the Lord.
King Bali, son of Virochana, said to him, "I give it." Knowing him to be Vamana, he gladly gave it himself.
That Lord Vamana, O best of brahmins, with three strides traversed heaven, sky and earth — this whole universe.
The Self of all beings surpassed the sun with his own splendour, illuminating all the directions and intermediate quarters, the glorious one.
The mighty-armed one shone, lighting up all the worlds; Janardana took away the Asuras' fortune and the three worlds,
and drove the Asuras with their sons and grandsons down to Patala. Namuchi, Shambara and Prahlada were, by Vishnu,
the cruel ones slain or driven off, and they took to the directions. Madhava, the Self of beings, the great elements with their particulars,
and Bali with his army, O brahmins — he showed a wonder there: in his body Bali beheld the whole world and himself.
There is nothing in the worlds not pervaded by that great soul. Seeing that form of Upendra, gods, Danavas and men
were all bewildered, dazed by Vishnu's splendour. Bali was bound with great nooses together with his kinsmen and friends.
The whole family of Virochana was settled in Patala. Then, having given the sovereignty over all the immortals to the great-souled Indra,
the mighty-armed Janardana appeared among men. These three are remembered as his auspicious divine manifestations.
Hear now of his seven human births along with their priests. In the tenth Treta age Dattatreya was born;
when dharma had perished, the fourth, with Markandeya as priest. The fifth was born in the fifteenth Treta age:
Mandhata, as universal emperor, with Utathya as priest. In the nineteenth Treta, the Lord who destroyed all the kshatriyas,
Jamadagnya, was the sixth, with Vishvamitra as priest. In the twenty-fourth age Rama, with Vasishtha as family priest,
the seventh, was born as son of Dasharatha for the sake of Ravana. The eighth, Vishnu in the twenty-eighth Dvapara, was born of Parashara
as Vedavyasa, with Jatukarnya as priest. Likewise the ninth, Vishnu — son of Aditi and Kashyapa —
was born of Devaki and Vasudeva, with Gargya as priest: immeasurable, the ordainer, fulfilling desires, self-controlled.
The Lord plays in the world like a child with toys. That mighty-armed Madhusudana cannot be measured.
There is nothing higher or lower than this universal form. So at the close of the twenty-eighth Dvapara,
when dharma perished, the Lord Vishnu was born in the Vrishni clan to establish dharma and destroy the Asuras, bewildering all beings with his yoga-maya, he whose self is yoga.
Having entered a human womb, he wanders the earth in disguise,
for his play among men, with Sandipani as his teacher. There Kamsa, Shalva and the great Asura Dvivida,
Arishta the bull, Putana, Keshin the horse, the elephant Kuvalayapida, the wrestler, and the lord of Rajagriha —
these Daityas dwelling in human bodies the mighty one destroyed. The thousand arms of Bana were cut off by that wondrous doer,
Naraka was slain in battle, and the mighty Yavana; all the jewels of the kings were taken by his might,
and the Kuru heroes and kings in Rasatala were slain. These are the manifestations of the great soul for the welfare of the world.
When this very age is waning and only its twilight remains, there will be the mighty Kalki named Vishnuyashas, of Parashara's line,
the tenth, yet to be born, with Yajnavalkya as priest. Leading an army crowded with elephants, horses and chariots,
surrounded by hundreds of thousands of brahmins bearing weapons, he will destroy those not truly righteous and those who hate dharma,
the northerners, the people of the middle country, those beyond the Vindhyas, the southerners and the Dravidas with the Sinhalas,
the Gandharas, Paradas, Pahlavas, Yavanas and Shakas, the Tusharas, Shabaras, Pulindas, Baradas and Vasas,
the Lampakas, Andhras, Pundras and Kiratas — that mighty Lord, turning the wheel of his rule, destroyer of the barbarians,
will roam the earth unseen by all beings. He was born as a man, son of the wise Devasena,
he who in a former birth was Vishnu, the mighty Pramiti, of the lineage of the Moon, at the close of the Kali age.
These are remembered as the manifestations of that god born through Daksha. For each such time, body and purpose,
he will enter those various wombs in the three worlds through a portion of himself. Established in the twenty-fifth kalpa for twenty-five years,
slaying all beings — men everywhere — and by cruel action leaving the earth with only a seed remaining,
having subdued the lowborn, who are mostly unrighteous, Kalki with his army will then have accomplished his purpose.
Those slain by his action will themselves be perfected again; suddenly enraged against one another, people will be deluded.
Having destroyed them all, impelled by what must be, he with his followers will come to rest between the Ganga and the Yamuna.
Then, when that period has passed and he and his army are gone, and the kings have perished, the people will be without restraint.
With protection gone, they will kill one another in fights, rob each other's property, joyless and deeply wretched.
Abandoning cities and villages, equal and without possessions, with the dharma of the scriptures and the stages of life lost,
short in stature and short-lived, they will dwell in forests, living by rivers and mountains and eating leaves, roots and fruits.
Wearing rags, leaves and skins, sunk in terrible confusion of classes, short-lived, without livelihood, beset by many troubles and deeply wretched —
having thus reached the extremity in the twilight portion of Kali, the people will perish along with the Kali age.
When that Kali age has ended and the Krita age begins again, they will return to right order by their own nature and not otherwise.
Thus all the doings of gods and Asuras have been told, and in connection with the Yadu line the great glory of Vishnu.
Now I shall tell of Turvasu, and of Puru, Druhyu and Anu.
Then, with a disciplined mind, he attained the abode of Brahma. Having attained brahminhood, Kakshivan begot a thousand sons.
Those sons of Kakshivan are remembered as the Kushmanda Gautamas. Thus has been told the meeting of Dirghatamas and Bali, son of Virochana,
and the offspring of both. Bali, having consecrated here his five sinless sons,
his purpose fulfilled, the lord whose self is yoga took to yoga and wanders unseen by all beings, awaiting his time.
There, in the line of the royal sage Anga, was King Dadhivahana. Because of an offence of Sudeshna, the king became Anapana.
Anapana's son is remembered as King Diviratha; Diviratha's son was the learned King Dharmaratha.
These Ikshvakus are said to be the kings of the Kali age, born in the line of Brihadbala, of great valour and prowess,
heroic, learned, true to their word and self-controlled. Here those who know the future cite this genealogical verse:
This line of the Ikshvakus will end with Sumitra; on reaching King Sumitra it will come to its close in the Kali age.
Thus the kshatriyas descended from Manu and from Ila have been described. Next I shall speak of Brihadratha of Magadha,
the kings in the line of Jarasandha, of Sahadeva's descent — past, present and future.
I shall tell of the principal ones; listen as I speak. In that Bharata war Sahadeva was slain.
His son Somapi, a royal sage, ruled at Girivraja for fifty-eight years.
His son Shrutashravas ruled sixty-seven years; Ayutayus reigned twenty-six years.
Niramitra enjoyed the earth for a hundred years and went to heaven; Sukshatra obtained the earth for fifty-six years.
Brihatkarman reigned twenty-three years; Senajit, now ruling, will enjoy as many years.
Shrutanjaya will rule forty years; then Ripunjaya, mighty-armed, of great intellect and prowess,
will protect the earth for thirty-five years; the pure one will remain on the throne for fifty-eight years.
Kshema will be king for a full twenty-eight years; the mighty Suvrata will obtain the kingdom for sixty-four.
Dharmanetra will reign for a full five years; the king will enjoy it for fifty-eight years.
The kingdom will be Sushrama's for thirty-eight years; Dridhasena will reign for forty-eight.
Then Sumati will obtain it for thirty-three years; then King Sunetra will enjoy it for forty years.
Satyajit will enjoy the earth and kingdom for eighty-three years; after him Vishvajit will reign for twenty-five.
Arinjaya will hold the earth for fifty years. These twenty-two kings will be the Brihadrathas;
their rule will last a full thousand years. When the Brihadrathas have passed, and the heroes and their successors are gone,
Shunaka will kill his master and forcibly consecrate his own son Pradyota as king before the eyes of the kshatriyas.
With vassals bowing to him, set in motion by what is to come, that best of men will be king for twenty-three years.
Then Palaka will be king for twenty-four years; Vishakhayupa will be king for fifty years.
The kingdom will be Ajaka's for twenty-one years; his son Nandivardhana will reign twenty years.
These five Pradyota kings will rule for a hundred and thirty-eight years. Destroying all their glory, Shishunaga will arise.
His son will be at Varanasi and will go to Girivraja. Shishunaga will reign forty years.
His son Kakavarna will reign thirty-six years; then Kshemadharman will be king for twenty.
Then Kshatraujas will obtain the kingdom for forty years; Vidhisara will be king for thirty-eight years.
Ajatashatru will be king for twenty-five years; Darbhaka will be king for thirty-five years.
After him Udayin will be king for thirty-three years. That king will build the excellent city called Kusuma on earth,
on the southern bank of the Ganga, in the fourth year. Nandivardhana will be king for forty years,
and Mahanandin for forty-three. Three hundred and sixty years in all
will these ten Shishunaga kings, kinsmen of the kshatriyas, reign. Along with them, for the same time, there will be other kings:
twenty-four Ikshvakus, twenty-five Panchalas, twenty-four Kalakas and twenty-four Haihayas,
thirty-two Ekalingas, twenty-five Shakas, thirty-six Kurus and twenty-eight Maithilas,
twenty-three Shurasenas and twenty Vitihotras — all these rulers of the earth will exist at the same time.
Mahanandin's son by a Shudra woman, driven by time, will arise: Mahapadma, the king who ends all kshatriyas.
From then on the kings will be of Shudra birth. That Mahapadma will be sole sovereign under a single umbrella.
He will rule the earth for eighty-eight years, having uprooted all the kshatriyas by the force of what must be.
After him his eight sons will be kings for twelve years; they will reign in succession after Mahapadma.
Kautilya, bull among brahmins, will uproot them all; having enjoyed the earth for a hundred years, that dynasty will pass.
Kautilya will establish Chandragupta as king; Chandragupta will reign twenty-four years.
Bhadrasara will be king for twenty-five years; then for thirty-six years the king who satisfies the Ashokas.
His son Kulala will reign eight years; Kushala's son Bandhupalita will also reign eight.
Bandhupalita's heir will be Indrapalita; Devavarman will be ruler for seven years.
His son will be King Shatadhanus; Brihadratha too will be king for seven years.
These nine Mauryas will enjoy the earth for a full hundred and thirty-seven years; from them it will pass to the Shungas.
The general Pushpamitra, having overthrown Brihadratha, will himself reign for sixty years.
King Agnimitra will reign eight years; then Sujyeshtha will reign seven years.
Then Vasumitra will be ruler for ten years; then Bhadra will be king for two years.
After him Pulindaka will reign three years; then King Ghosha will reign three years.
Then Vajramitra will be king for seven years; then King Bhagavata will reign thirty-two years.
His son Devabhumi will reign ten years. These ten Shunga kings will enjoy this earth
for a full hundred and twelve years; from them it will pass to the Kanvas. The minister Vasudeva, the king being given to vice from youth,
will kill Devabhumi and become king among the Shungas; that Kanvayana will reign five years.
His son Bhumimitra will reign twenty-four years; after him King Narayana will reign twelve years.
His son Susharman will reign four years. These four Kanvayanas will rule forty-five years
and enjoy the earth; then it will pass to the Andhras. Having forcibly overthrown the Kanvayana Susharman,
Sindhuka of the Andhra race will obtain this earth; Sindhuka will be king for twenty-three years.
His brother Krishna will reign ten years after him; his son will be the great Shri Shantakarni.
Shantakarni will reign fifty-six years; his son Apolava will reign twelve.
Patuman will reign twenty-four years; Anishtakarman will reign twenty-five years.
Then Hala will be king for a full year; then the mighty one named Panchapattalaka.
Purishabhiru will reign twenty-one years; Shatakarni will be ruler for one year.
Shivasvati will reign twenty-eight years; King Gautamiputra will reign twenty-one years.
Then King Yajna Shri Shatakarni will reign nineteen years; after him Vijaya will reign six years.
His son Deda Shri Shatakarni will reign three years; then Pulomari will reign seven years among them.
These thirty Andhra kings will enjoy the earth for four hundred and fifty-six years.
When the Andhras have come to an end, there will be five of their kinsmen; then seven kings, and ten Abhira kings,
seven Gardabhins, then ten Shakas; eight Yavanas will follow, and fourteen Tusharas,
thirteen Gurundas and eleven Maunas. The Andhras will enjoy the earth for three hundred years,
and the ten Abhira kings for sixty-seven years; the seven Gardabhins will enjoy it for seventy-two years.
The Shakas will enjoy the earth for three hundred and eighty years; the Yavanas will enjoy the earth for eighty-two years.
The earth is remembered as belonging to the Tusharas for five hundred years; the thirteen will rule for three hundred and fifty years.
The Gurundas, of barbarian race, will enjoy it along with the lowborn; the eleven Maunas will enjoy it for three hundred years.
When they are cut off by time, then the Kilakila kings will arise; after the Kilakilas, Vindhyashakti will arise
and will hold the earth for ninety-six years. Now hear of the future kings of Vidisha.
Son of Shesha, king of the Nagas, will be Purañjaya, a prince of the gods; Bhogin will be king, upholder of the Naga line.
Sadachandra, then Chandramshu the second, then Nakhavan, then Dhanadharman, remembered as the fourth of the line.
Then Bhutinanda will rule in Vidisha; his younger brother was named Nandiyashas.
Three kings will be of his line. His daughter's son, named Shishika, became king in Purika.
Vindhyashakti's son, the mighty Pravira, will enjoy the city of Kanchanaka for sixty years.
He will perform Vajapeya sacrifices with excellent fees; his four sons will become kings.
Three kings will be related by marriage to the Vindhyaka families. Supratika and Gabhira will reign twenty years.
Shankamana became king, lord of the Mahishis. There will be six Pushpamitras and thirteen Strimitras.
In Mekala there will be seven kings, ruling seventy years; in Komala there will be mighty kings,
nine wise ones known as the Meghas. All the kings of Nishadha, until the end of the Manu period,
will be born of the line of Nala, mighty and powerful. Among the Magadhas the very mighty Vishvasphani will arise.
Uprooting all the kings, he will raise other classes: Kaivartas, Madrakas, Pulindas and brahmins.
Those kings will settle people in various lands. Vishvasphani, of great strength, equal in splendour to Vishnu in battle —
King Vishvasphani is said to look like a eunuch; uprooting the kshatriyas, he will create another warrior class.
Nine Naga kings will enjoy the city of Champavati, and seven Nagas will enjoy the lovely city of Mathura.
The lands along the Ganga, Prayaga, Saketa and the Magadhas — all these lands will be enjoyed by the seven lineages.
The Naishadhas, Yadukas, Shaishitas and Kalatoyakas — all these lands will be enjoyed by those born of Manidhanya.
The Koshalas, Andhras, Paundras and Tamraliptas with the coasts, and the lovely city of Champa, will be enjoyed by the Devarakshitas.
The Kalingas, the Mahishas and those dwelling on Mahendra — all these lands Guha will protect.
Kanaka will enjoy Striraashtra and the Bhojakas. All these rulers of the earth will exist at the same time.
Of little grace, untruthful, very wrathful and unrighteous, there will be Yavanas here in dharma, desire and wealth.
These rulers will not be consecrated kings; corrupted by the faults of the age, they will be of evil conduct.
In the course of time such rulers of the earth will arise here, devoid of dharma, desire and wealth.
The lands mixed with them will follow barbarian customs everywhere; living in perversity, they will destroy the people.
The kings then will be greedy and untruthful; in their turn the age will be full of many women.
Declining little by little in lifespan, beauty, strength and learning — when the people have reached that extreme, the lords of the world,
the kings, will perish, struck down by time. Slain by Kalki, all the barbarians will go to destruction,
along with those who are utterly unrighteous and heretics everywhere. When the very name of king has perished, in the twilight remnant of the Kali age,
the few people remaining, with dharma lost and possessions gone, without means, robbed, afflicted by disease and grief,
struck by drought and by killing one another,
without support, terrified, giving up their livelihood in misery, abandoning cities and villages, will become forest-dwellers.
When such things perish, the people will leave their homes; affection lost, in dire straits, friends estranged,
fallen from the order of classes and stages of life, sunk in dreadful confusion, the people will then live by rivers and mountains.
They will resort to rivers, coastal marshes and mountains; to Anga, Kalinga, Vanga, Kashmir, Kashi and Koshala;
men will take shelter in the valleys of the Rishika mountains, the whole slope of the Himalaya and the shore of the salt sea.
Aryans along with barbarians will go into the forest; with deer, fish, birds, beasts of prey and sugarcane,
and with honey, vegetables, fruits and roots, men will sustain themselves. Rags, leaves of various kinds, bark and skins
they will make themselves and wear, like hermits. They will sow grain in hollows with wooden stakes,
and carefully tend goats, sheep, donkeys and camels. Men will surely settle by rivers for the sake of water.
The rulers will oppress one another in their dealings; conceited, without offspring, devoid of purity and good conduct —
so will men be then, established in adharma; the people will follow the base, the wretched and the unrighteous.
Then no one's life will exceed twenty-three years; weak, wearied by sense-pleasures, overwhelmed by old age,
eating leaves, roots and fruits, dressed in rags and black antelope skins, they will roam the earth seeking a livelihood.
The people will reach this state at the end of the Kali age. When that Kali age of a thousand divine years has waned,
they will perish completely along with the Kali age. When its twilight portion has wholly ended, the Krita age will begin.
When the moon, the sun, Tishya and Jupiter are together in one sign, then the Krita age will come.
This entire sequence of dynasties has been told to you in order — those past, present and yet to come.
From the birth of Parikshit to the coronation of Mahananda, this should be known as one thousand and fifty years.
And to state the measure from Mahapadma onward, the interval is remembered as eight hundred and thirty-six years.
This interval of time is to come; those beginning and ending with the Andhras have been named, counted by sages learned in the Puranas and the scriptures.
The Seven Sages were then in the Pitrya asterism in Parikshit's time for a hundred years; after twenty-seven hundred years the lineages of the Andhras will come again.
Through the whole circle of twenty-seven asterisms, the Seven Sages stay in turn a hundred years in each.
This is remembered as the age of the Seven Sages in divine reckoning: six divine months and seven divine years.
From them proceeds divine time, through those Seven Sages. Of the Seven Sages, the two foremost seen in the northern sky —
the asterism seen midway between them in the heavens is the one with which the Seven Sages should be known to be joined in the sky for a hundred years.
This illustrates the period of occupancy of the asterisms by the sages. The Seven Sages were so joined for a hundred years in Parikshit's time.
At the twenty-fourth portion of the Andhras they will be for a hundred years. Then these people will fall into deep calamity,
all struck by falsehood in dharma, desire and wealth. When the dharma of the Vedas and Smritis, of classes and stages of life, has grown lax,
the weak-minded, deluded, will fall into confusion; Shudras will mingle with the twice-born.
Brahmins will perform sacrifices for Shudras, and Shudras will be sources of mantras; brahmins seeking livelihood by bad conduct will then serve them.
Declining little by little, all the people in due course will go to destruction, with only a remnant left at the end of the age.

Kali is said to last three hundred and sixty thousand years by human reckoning.
A thousand divine years are declared, with its twilight portion; when that has wholly ended, the Krita age will begin.
The lines of Aila and of Ikshvaku have been told with their branches. The kshatriya line of Ikshvaku, son of Vivasvan, is remembered as ending with Sumitra;
those who know the lunar line know the Aila kshatriya line to end with Kshemaka. These sons of Vivasvan have been told, increasers of fame.
Those past, present and to come — brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras remembered here —
great souls have passed by thousands in age after age. Because the names in each family are so many,
and because of much repetition, I have not enumerated them all. In this Vaivasvata interval the line of Nimi does not come to an end.
Since the kshatriya order will arise again in this age, I shall tell how; listen as I speak.
Devapi, the Paurava king, and Maru of the Ikshvaku line, endowed with great yogic power, dwell in the village of Kalapa.
These two will be founders of the kshatriyas in the twenty-fourth cycle of four ages. A son named Suvarchas will be born of Ikshvaku's line;
in the twenty-ninth age he will be the founder of the dynasty. From Devapi's line will come the first king of the Aila line.
These two will be founders of the kshatriyas in that cycle of ages. Thus everywhere this is to be understood as the mark of lineage continuity.
When that Kali age has ended, in the future Krita age, and again in the first Treta age, together with those Seven Sages,
they will be the founders of the clans and of the kshatriyas. By a portion of Dvapara the kshatriyas remain together with the sages.
